How SIU keeps football players safe in extreme heat
CARBONDALE, Ill. (KFVS) - High temperatures are changing the way athletes are practicing this week.

Skip to contentHow SIU keeps football players safe in extreme heat
And the SIU Salukis football program is making adjustments to help athletes stay safe while training in the extreme heat.
It’s nearly football season, and the players are back for preseason. With this heat, the goal is simple: make sure athletes are ready to compete without putting their health at risk.
Head Football Trainer Mike Lyznicki is busy making sure his players are hydrated and recovering well as they move closer to the season.
Because of the heat, football practices have been shifted to start before the hottest parts of the afternoon.
“We ended up moving up a couple hours just to make sure the guys were getting on the team to make sure it’s safe for them to be out there practicing in their football equipment,” Lyznicki said.
Extra precautions matter because high heat and humidity can quickly turn dangerous. Lyznicki said when it’s humid and hot, it can affect the athlete’s ability to sweat, and sweat is how they cool down their body.
“If they’re not able to sweat and they’re out there in direct sunlight, then we can run into some exertional heat illness, heat exhaustion, heat stroke,” Lyznicki said.
For players, those risks aren’t just theoretical. SIU Athletic Director Tim Leonard shared an experience from his previous institution.
“We had a young man that happened in fall camp out in the heat and humidity and fell down with a heat stroke. Technically, he passed away twice, flatlined twice. Fortunately, our sports medicine crew and our athletic trainers had a catastrophic injury plan. They knew exactly what to do, and they revived him. They got him into the cold tubs right away, prepped him for emergency vehicles to arrive, and got him to the hospital. It was touch and go, and obviously, he flatlined, but they were able to revive him, and he was able to make a full recovery.”
The close calls are why Leonard says colleges have those emergency plans in place and guidelines they have to follow. He said he has to make sure they have a catastrophic injury plan in place and are ready to go.
“But heat stroke is not something to mess around with, and it can occur when it’s this hot and humid out, and you have to take it seriously and be prepared,” he said.
“We know what would happen should anything like that happen. Can we react quickly? Could we get emergency vehicles in and out on a quick basis and all those types of things,” Leonard added.
To make sure the worst does not happen, Lyznicki says focusing on prevention and recovery is very important. He said they monitor their meals, calorie intake and always make sure they have enough fluids at practice.
“Enough breaks to have those fluids and make sure that they’re getting enough time to cool off between reps and that type,” he said.
For the Salukis, staying hydrated is key to staying safe and performing at their best in the summer heat. Trainers say that advice doesn’t just apply to athletes—it applies to everyone spending time outdoors.

Extreme heat puts firefighters at risk alongside every emergency

Skip to contentExtreme heat puts firefighters at risk alongside every emergency
CAPE GIRARDEAU, Mo. (KFVS) - Firefighters in the Heartland are taking additional steps to protect crews from heat exhaustion as extreme temperatures strain emergency responders on scene.
Assistant Fire Chief Garrett Schott of Perryville said extreme heat drains crews quickly, prompting his station to call mutual aid on nearly every run.
At a recent silo fire, medical personnel evaluated firefighters on scene for heat exhaustion and heat-related stress.
“They took the guys, they put them there making sure their vital signs were good, we got them on fluids, as far as drinking lots of water, we also carry on our trucks Liquid IV and fire salt that they can put in their water bottles to help them with dehydration,” Schott said.
Cape Girardeau EMS Assistant Director Harry Myers said firefighters face heightened risk from the combination of their environment and heavy equipment.
“At the scene of a fire, they are actively on scene, wearing all their gear, which can weigh up to 80 pounds, so that, combined with the weather, takes a major toll on them, so it’s important that they are keeping cool, drinking lots of water,” he said.
Myers said he frequently runs water and ice to crews during calls to keep them cool and hydrated between responses.
“It’s all about staying hydrated, knowing when you feel like you need to get inside, get cool, or take a break—that’s why it’s so important on scene to swap out and take breaks,” Myers said.
Schott said his station is requesting extra crews on emergency calls to rotate with firefighters and reduce the risk of heat-related injury.
“Most of the time in this heat, they are doing maybe 10 to 15 minutes on an air bottle, then they are coming right into rehab to get some fluids in them and try to get them fresh,” he said.
Both Schott and Meyers said it’s important for everyone to avoid the extreme heat whenever you can, and drink as many fluids as possible to stay hydrated.

Heavy rain hits Delhi-NCR: IMD issues orange alert as monsoon intensifies
A shift in atmospheric conditions has changed the weather over Delhi-NCR. Here's what is driving the change and what people can expect through the rest of the week.

A traffic police personnel regulates vehicular movement on a road amid rain in Delhi. (Photo: PTI)
People in Delhi-NCR woke up to overcast skies and scattered showers on Tuesday, July 28, a weather shift that brought relief from the uncomfortable humidity that has persisted for days.
After patchy rain earlier this month, a fresh spell of monsoon showers returned, with the IMD issuing an orange alert for continued rain in the next few hours.
Meteorologists further noted that the first morning spell of rain had moved east from Delhi and east NCR, leaving only light drizzle in some spots.
Fresh thunderstorms are expected to build over Haryana by afternoon, triggering more rain and storms across Delhi-NCR through the evening.
WHY DID MONSOON RAIN RETURN TO DELHI-NCR?
This rain revival comes from a deep depression, which is basically a large, slow-moving low-pressure weather system that formed over the northwest Bay of Bengal and moved inland across Odisha and West Bengal.
The giant system often acts like a pump, drawing warm, moisture-laden winds from the sea and carries it northward over central and northern India, bringing rain.
This system strengthens the monsoon trough, an elongated belt of low pressure that normally runs across northern India during the rainy season.
When the trough sits in its usual position over the plains near Delhi, it pulls air upward. Rising air cools, moisture condenses into clouds, and rain falls, sometimes accompanied by thunderstorms.
Rain "bands" are simply organised lines or strips of heavier showers within the broader cloudy area, moving in a specific direction.
Flat plains like Delhi-NCR spread rain more evenly, while hilly areas further north force the same moist air upward sharply, producing even heavier downpours.
Earlier weeks brought more isolated or scattered showers because the trough was often positioned farther away, leading to humid but drier conditions despite cloudy skies.
The current active phase is boosted by extra swirling low-pressure areas, commonly known as cyclonic circulations, over places like Rajasthan.
In recent decades, Delhi's monsoon rains have shifted toward shorter, more intense thunderstorm bursts rather than steady, all-day drizzle, a change linked to evolving weather patterns and urban influences.
WILL IT RAIN IN THE COMING DAYS?
While the rains have grown less steady, this spell has brought better news.

The India Meteorological Department (IMD) has also issued a yellow alert for Wednesday, meaning generally cloudy skies with spells of light to moderate rain and thunderstorms shall persist until tomorrow.
Daytime highs should stay cooler at 32-35°C, down from recent peaks near 38°C.
Similar rainy conditions are likely to continue into Thursday and the weekend, helping close any monsoon shortfall for the month.
This active spell shows how a single weather system hundreds of kilometres away can quickly transform conditions over the northern plains by feeding steady moisture into the monsoon trough.

THIRUVANANTHAPURAM: Rains are intensifying in the state again. Many places including the capital city received heavy rains Tuesday morning. The India Meteorological Department (IMD) has informed that there is a possibility of isolated rains with thunderstorms and strong winds with a speed of up to 40 kmph in Thiruvananthapuram, Kollam, Pathanamthitta, Alappuzha, Kottayam, Idukki, Ernakulam, Thrissur and Palakkad in the next few hours.
Yellow alert has been issued for Ernakulam, Thrissur, Malappuram, Kozhikode, Kannur and Kasaragod today. The possibility of isolated heavy rains has been predicted. Heavy rains are defined as a situation where 64.5 mm to 115.5 mm of rain is expected in 24 hours.
The extreme low-pressure area located over the north-west Bay of Bengal and the West Bengal-north Odisha coasts has intensified into an extremely severe low-pressure area. The IMD has informed that it is likely to move in a north-northwesterly direction and make landfall between Balasore and Canning on the West Bengal-North Odisha coast. The cyclonic circulation is located over the East Arabian Sea and the nearby Konkan coast. There is a possibility of rain in Kerala till July 31 due to this, informed the IMD.
